Pullrun Unifies Container and VM Execution with Single OCI Image Support

Pullrun is a new AI development that collapses multiple execution engines into a single runtime, enabling the same OCI image to run as a container, Firecracker microVM, Apple Silicon VM, Kubernetes workload, or AI agent task. Modern infrastructure relies on disparate tools—Docker for development, containerd for production, Firecracker for isolation, and MCP agents for AI—each with separate image formats and storage models. item.title: Updates on Production-Grade Microservice Boilerplates and Wazuh Security Platform
item.description:
Updates on Production-Grade Microservice Boilerplates and Wazuh Security Platform

Recent developments highlight updates regarding a production-grade microservice boilerplate and the features of the Wazuh open-source security platform.

🔍 Overview

A production-grade microservice boilerplate has been introduced, featuring tools such as GORM, Goose, Swag, Zerolog, Validator.v10, GitOps, Kubernetes, Kustomize, ArgoCD, and Istio. Additionally, Wazuh continues to serve as a free and open-source platform used for threat prevention, detection, and response across on-premises, virtualized, containerized, and cloud-based environments.

⚙️ Key details

  • The microservice boilerplate builds a production-ready containerized RESTful API server application using Go standard library net/http and the Chi router.
  • Development environments use golang:1.27-alpine (~1180 MB) and postgres:19-alpine (~440 MB), while production uses distroless/static-debian13:nonroot (~46 MB).
  • For high-traffic systems with large PostgreSQL tables, arranging fixed-width columns by decreasing alignment requirements can reduce tuple alignment padding and potentially minimize storage size, a technique called “Column Tetris”.
  • Wazuh’s architecture consists of an endpoint security agent and a management server.
  • Wazuh agents scan monitored systems for malware, rootkits, suspicious anomalies, hidden files, cloaked processes, and unregistered network listeners.
  • The Wazuh server uses a signature-based approach to intrusion detection with a regular expression engine.
  • Wazuh provides native integration with the Docker engine to monitor images, volumes, network settings, and running containers.
  • Cloud infrastructure monitoring includes integration modules for Amazon AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

💡 Why it matters

These tools help organizations build robust containerized RESTful APIs with automated GitOps deployment via ArgoCD, while maintaining comprehensive security, threat detection, and regulatory compliance with standards such as PCI DSS, GPG13, and GDPR using Wazuh.

#Microservices #Go #Kubernetes #Security #Wazuh

item.title: Kong Gateway introduces AI traffic capabilities and MCP governance
item.description:
Kong Gateway introduces AI traffic capabilities and MCP governance

Kong or Kong Gateway is a cloud-native, platform-agnostic, scalable API, LLM, and MCP Gateway distinguished for its high performance and extensibility via plugins. It provides advanced AI traffic capabilities with multi-LLM support, semantic security, MCP traffic security and analytics, and more.

🔍 Overview

Kong serves as the central layer for orchestrating microservices or conventional API traffic - and agentic LLM and MCP as well - with ease. By providing functionality for proxying, routing, load balancing, health checking, and authentication, it manages traffic across various architectures.

⚙️ Key details

  • Universal LLM API: Routes traffic across multiple providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, GCP Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure AI, Databricks, Mistral, and Huggingface.
  • MCP Capabilities: Includes MCP traffic governance, security, observability, and autogeneration from any RESTful API.
  • AI Features: Offers over 60 features such as AI observability, semantic security, caching, and semantic routing.
  • Security and Routing: Supports authentication and authorization via JWT, basic auth, OAuth, and ACLs.
  • Traffic Management: Handles proxying, SSL/TLS termination, and connectivity support for L4 or L7 traffic.
  • Plugins: Includes 60+ plugins for traffic controls, rate limiting, request/response transformations, logging, and monitoring.
Feature Description
Advanced Routing Load balancing and health checking configurable via RESTful admin API or declarative configuration
Deployment Models Supports Declarative Databaseless Deployment and Hybrid Deployment with control plane/data plane separation
Kubernetes Support Runs natively on Kubernetes thanks to its official Kubernetes Ingress Controller
Plugin Hub Showcases Kong Inc. and community-developed plugins like AWS Lambda, Correlation ID, and Response Transformer

🚀 Availability

Kong is available in various distributions depending on the deployment environment. Users can run it in the cloud, on bare metal, or using containers.

  • Cloud: Sign up for a free trial of Kong Konnect to get started with a cloud-hosted solution.
  • Docker: The docker-compose distribution is suggested for easy setup. A docker installation procedure is also available for running the Kong Gateway in DB-less mode.
  • Installation: To start with the Docker distribution, clone the Docker repository and navigate to the compose folder. Use the command $ KONG_DATABASE=postgres docker-compose --profile database up to start the Gateway stack.

Once started, the Gateway is available on localhost with the following ports:

  • 8000: Send traffic to your service via Kong.
  • 8001: Configure Kong using Admin API or via decK.
  • 8002: Access Kong’s management Web UI (Kong Manager).

#Kong #APIGateway #MCP #LLM #Kubernetes #DevOps

item.title: Weaviate Helm Chart v17.1.0: Raft Bootstrap and Resource Limit Changes
item.description:
Weaviate Helm Chart v17.1.0: Raft Bootstrap and Resource Limit Changes

The Weaviate Helm chart has released version 17.1.0, introducing significant updates to cluster bootstrapping in Weaviate v1.25 and removing default resource constraints to improve module performance.

🔍 Overview

Weaviate can be deployed to a Kubernetes cluster using the provided Helm chart, provided that Helm is installed. Version 17.1.0 of the chart addresses specific infrastructure changes required by newer Weaviate releases and resolves performance restrictions in default configurations.

⚙️ Key Details: Cluster Bootstrapping

Weaviate v1.25 introduced a significant change in how the cluster bootstraps, driven by the adoption of a Raft-based consensus model.

  • The podManagementPolicy was changed from OrderedReady to Parallel.
  • This change is required for the Raft cluster to bootstrap properly, as all pods must start simultaneously.
  • Once the Raft cluster is established, rolling updates are possible.
  • This change takes effect when migrating from versions prior to v1.25 or when bootstrapping a new v1.25 cluster.

⚠️ Migration Steps

When upgrading from a version older than v1.25 to v1.25 or above, the following one-time operation is required:

  1. Delete Weaviate’s Statefulset.
  2. Update the Statefulset settings to reflect the new policy.

This process will not remove your data but is necessary to make the update of Statefulset settings possible.

📉 Key Details: Resource Limits

In Weaviate-Helm version 17.1.0, the default resource limits and requests defined in the values.yml file have been removed.

  • Reason: Previous default values restricted the performance of some modules, making them almost unusable unless resources.requests and resources.limits were overridden.
  • Impact: Modules deployed with default values prior to version 17.1.0 will have their resource values removed upon upgrading to 17.1.0 or above, resulting in no constraints on memory or CPU usage.
  • Recommendation: To prevent modules from consuming all system resources, users are strongly recommended to override modules.$MODULE.resources.requests and modules.$MODULE.resources.limits with values that suit their specific system.

🛠 Release Process

To release a new version of the chart, the following steps are taken:

  • Bump the chart version in ./weaviate/Chart.yaml.
  • Create a commit and an annotated tag matching the version number (prefixed with v, e.g., v1.4.3).
  • Push the commit and tag to the repository.
  • A GitHub Action creates a drafted release with the packaged chart attached.
  • The draft is edited to include release notes and published.

#Weaviate #Kubernetes #Helm #VectorDB #DevOps

item.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Introduces Workload Recovery and Infrastructure Checks
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Introduces Workload Recovery and Infrastructure Checks

Today, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod introduces workload recovery and infrastructure checks. These features catch failures sooner and raise the goodput of training workloads.

🧩 The Challenge

Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy. A GPU with a subtle fault can pass its stress tests and still return wrong values. When a job stalls on an NCCL timeout, it keeps its GPUs, and Slurm still shows it as running. If a device plugin crashes on one node, the job fails with an error that never mentions the plugin.

Teams usually find these problems only after the loss diverges or the job fails, and by then, the compute is spent. Each of these failures lowers goodput, the share of your cluster’s time that goes to useful training.

Types of Failures

  • Numerical faults: A GPU can pass every hardware test and still compute wrong results. The first sign is often NaN or infinite loss in a production run.
  • Hung jobs: An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can stop a job without ending it. The job keeps its GPUs and their memory, and Slurm reports it as running until someone checks the loss curve or the log.
  • Cluster-level failures: Some failures happen in Kubernetes, not in a node’s hardware. A device plugin crash-loops, a required DaemonSet never starts on a new node, or ranks on different nodes fall out of step in an NCCL collective. When the job fails, the error often doesn’t say which pod or node caused it.

🛡️ New Infrastructure Checks

The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors, deep health checks test nodes during provisioning, and automatic node recovery reboots or replaces faulty hardware.

Monitoring Agents and Checks

Feature Description
Health Monitoring Agent (HMA) Watches each node for GPU errors such as Xid and NVLink faults, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) errors, and kernel errors.
MultiNodeTrainingValidation A new deep health check for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When HyperPod provisions an instance, or when you run the check on demand, it trains a small model on the instance and then across instances of the same type. The instance fails if the loss becomes NaN or infinite, or training doesn’t finish in time.
Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent Watches the Kubernetes layer of an EKS cluster for problems such as crash-looping device plugins, missing DaemonSets, and tainted nodes. When a job fails, it reports the pods and nodes involved as Kubernetes events and Amazon CloudWatch logs.
Hung Job Detection Finds Slurm jobs that have stopped making progress. An agent on each node watches the job’s output and GPU activity, or log patterns that you define. It writes an event to CloudWatch and can cancel the job so that Slurm requeues it.

⚙️ Existing Resiliency Features

The existing HyperPod resiliency features check a single node at a time.

  • InstanceStress: Runs DCGM level 4 diagnostics and tests each instance’s GPUs, GPU memory, NVLink, and EFA devices.
  • InstanceConnectivity: Runs NCCL tests across GPU instances, or NCCOM tests on AWS Trainium.

🚀 Availability

These checks run when instances are provisioned, or on demand, and confirm that their GPUs train correctly. Hung job detection runs alongside each Slurm job and catches a job that has stopped making progress.

#SageMakerHyperPod #MachineLearning #GPUComputing #Kubernetes #AWSInfrastructure

Source: Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Amazon Web Services

item.title: NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning Enables Shared GPU Memory on EKS
item.description:
NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning Enables Shared GPU Memory on EKS

NVIDIA has open-sourced Run:ai, an AI workload orchestration platform for Kubernetes, and validated a GPU Fractioning capability that allows multiple Pods to share a single GPU on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). In the validated example, two Pods successfully shared one NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU on an EC2 g5.xlarge instance, each allocating 6 GiB within an 8 GiB memory limit while an allocation above the limit was rejected as expected.

🔍 Overview

GPU sharing is not new — Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) address different isolation and utilization needs. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning builds on MPS with Kubernetes-integrated scheduling, per-Pod memory contracts, enforcement, and metrics. The GPU Fractioning Operator helps several teams share one or two GPUs, addressing scenarios where notebooks, model evaluations, and small inference services leave teams waiting even when GPU memory remains available.

🧩 How it works

In the baseline configuration, the NVIDIA device plugin exposes a single GPU as one nvidia.com/gpu resource with GPU sharing disabled. Two Pods each requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 cannot run concurrently on that node, even when their combined GPU-memory demand fits. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds:

  • Kubernetes scheduling integration via the KAI Scheduler
  • Enforced GPU-memory limits per Pod
  • Per-Pod GPU-memory metrics

The approach applies to NVIDIA GPUs that meet the GPU Fractioning Operator’s hardware and software requirements, including GPUs without MIG. It uses NvFractions annotations, not Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA).

⚙️ Key details

Component Detail
Validated GPU NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU (23,028 MiB)
Validated instance Amazon EC2 g5.xlarge
System node m7i.large hosting operator controllers and KAI Scheduler
GPU worker OS Custom Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023)
GPU driver NVIDIA R615 driver branch
Container runtime containerd with NVIDIA Container Toolkit
Sharing mechanism MPS via fractiond with Node Resource Interface (NRI) integration
Metrics collection metricsd daemon exports per-Pod GPU-memory metrics
Compute modes Time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing
Error domains Separate workload error domains for default mode; shared error domain for sm-sharing (not security guarantees)

Each Pod receives an 8 GiB GPU-memory limit and allocates 6 GiB. The KAI Scheduler places both Pods on a tainted g5.xlarge node. The walkthrough establishes a whole-GPU baseline, verifies 6 GiB allocations, inspects per-Pod metrics, tests rejection of a 9 GiB allocation, and cleans up the disposable environment.

🚀 Availability

NVIDIA announced the open source release of NVIDIA Run:ai on October 13, 2026. This walkthrough uses two of its four modular components: KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator. KAI Resource Management and Workload Map address organizational governance and additional workload types, outside this walkthrough’s scope. Other configurations require compatibility checks and validation.

💡 Why it matters

Choose GPU fractioning when you need enforced per-Pod GPU-memory limits on GPUs without MIG and can run fixed-size GPU node groups. A memory limit does not reserve proportional compute. This walkthrough tests memory limits, not fault containment or compute performance. The solution enables better GPU utilization for workloads that don’t require a full GPU, reducing wait times for development and inference tasks.

#NVIDIA #Kubernetes #GPU #EKS #AI #Run:ai

Source: Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS | Amazon Web Services

item.title: New Structural-Validation Evaluation Harness for Java LLM Codegen Service
item.description:
New Structural-Validation Evaluation Harness for Java LLM Codegen Service

📚 Introduction

A new structural-validation evaluation harness has been introduced for a Java LLM codegen service, designed to make A/B changes measurable and provide deterministic metrics instead of relying on demo screenshots or subjective assessments.

🔍 Overview

The harness implements a two-tier evaluation approach:

  • Runs benchmark prompts against a local Java service
  • Captures generated code through SSE
  • Evaluates outputs with deterministic structural checks
  • Optional browser execution smoke checks
  • Records raw JSON plus Markdown reports
  • Attributes tokens with per-run Prometheus counter windows

The most important finding was not a token percentage but a discovered issue: an earlier token result was polluted by Redis MessageWindowChatMemory carryover on a shared appId.

🧩 How it Works

The evaluation system operates through several components:

  • Kubernetes manifests serve Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B through vLLM
  • Infrastructure spans infra/azure (AKS/ACR/node pools) and infra/workloads (Terraform-managed inference/evaluation workloads)
  • A read-only authenticated GraphQL API queries both legacy Java reports and new serving runs
  • A bounded-concurrency benchmark records TTFT, p50/p95 latency, request/token throughput and structural quality

⚙️ Key Details

The structural pass@k evaluation found:

Metric Result
Structural pass@3 90.0% -> 90.0%
Total tokens 323,192 -> 317,785 (-1.7%)
CodeGen-stage input reduction ~18%

The harness identified a Java product bug: loadChatHistoryToMemory(...) returned before chatMemory.clear() when MySQL history was empty, causing prompt-composition diagnostics to reveal most of the CodeGen prompt was carried-over history.

Additional capabilities include:

  • Optional direct OpenAI-compatible inference reusing HTML evaluators and raw result format
  • Execution smoke checker validates known browser fixtures
  • One-shot repair path validates on a deterministic fixture
  • Replay / fixture mode validates offline report and evaluator paths
  • Failure taxonomy classifies report failures by layer

🚀 Availability

Documentation is available in three parts:

  • Part 1 deployment and recording guide
  • Part 2 Azure guide
  • Part 3 query and recording guide

Additional references:

  • RESULTS.md for full claim audit
  • Redis chat-memory carryover postmortem for incident write-up
  • LoRA/QLoRA SFT and held-out evaluation for deterministic data preparation and training provenance

💡 Why It Matters

The structural-validation pass@k differs from HumanEval-style evaluation:

  • It measures deterministic structural correctness, not functional correctness
  • Execution smoke validation serves as a thin second layer for narrow browser/build sanity, not full functional testing
  • The two layers are reported separately to avoid collapsing into one ambiguous pass number

Implementation tests are offline, and actual GPU deployment and performance measurements are pending. The sample data serves as a pipeline smoke fixture, with GPU training and quality gains remaining unverified.

#LLM #Evaluation #CodeGeneration #Java #DevOps #Kubernetes

item.title: Flux v2 and GitOps Toolkit Launch for Kubernetes
item.description:
Flux v2 and GitOps Toolkit Launch for Kubernetes

Flux version 2 (v2) has been released, built from the ground up to use the Kubernetes API extension system. It integrates with the GitOps Toolkit, a set of composable APIs and specialized tools designed for building continuous delivery on top of Kubernetes.

🔍 Overview

Flux is an open and extensible continuous delivery solution for Kubernetes that keeps clusters in sync with sources of configuration, such as Git repositories and OCI artifacts. It automates updates to configuration when there is new code to deploy. The project is a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) graduated project, used in production by various organizations and cloud providers.

🧩 How it works

The GitOps Toolkit consists of the APIs and controllers that make up the runtime for Flux v2. These APIs comprise Kubernetes custom resources, which can be created and updated by cluster users or other automation tooling. Flux v2 is constructed to integrate with Prometheus and other core components of the Kubernetes ecosystem.

⚙️ Key details

Version 2 introduces several long-requested features, including:

  • Support for multi-tenancy
  • Ability to sync an arbitrary number of Git repositories
  • Extensibility through the composable APIs of the GitOps Toolkit

Users can use the toolkit to extend Flux or to build custom systems for continuous delivery.

🚀 Availability

To get started, users can refer to the available guide on how to bootstrap Flux on Kubernetes and deploy a sample application in a GitOps manner. Developer guides are also available for those wishing to build their own systems using the toolkit.

#Kubernetes #GitOps #ContinuousDelivery #Flux #CNCF

Source: fluxcd/flux2

item.title: LLMKube Unifies LLM Inference Across GPU Fleets
item.description:
LLMKube Unifies LLM Inference Across GPU Fleets

LLMKube is a Kubernetes operator that manages LLM inference across heterogeneous GPU fleets, including NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple Silicon hosts. It turns deployment into a two-resource YAML setup and can expose models through an OpenAI-compatible API.

🔍 Overview

Define a Model and an InferenceService; the operator handles model downloading and caching, GPU scheduling, health checks, scaling, and API exposure. Linux GPU pods and Apple Silicon hosts both appear as InferenceService objects to kubectl.

🧩 How it works

The system has two cooperating processes:

  • An in-cluster controller manages Kubernetes-side desired state.
  • An optional out-of-cluster metal-agent is used for Apple Silicon hosts. It supervises OS-level processes and registers authenticated ingress with the cluster. An in-cluster relay fronts that ingress, so Metal InferenceService objects are ordinary Services.

On Apple Silicon, inference runs as native macOS processes rather than containers, allowing full Metal GPU access.

⚙️ Supported hardware and runtimes

Hardware or runtime Details in the evidence
NVIDIA CUDA support
AMD Vulkan support
Intel Listed among supported heterogeneous fleet hosts
Apple Silicon Metal support; native macOS inference processes
Runtimes llama.cpp, vLLM, TGI, and mlx-server
Apple Silicon processes The Metal Agent runs llama-server, mlx-server, and vllm-swift

Other capabilities include multi-GPU sharding, model caching, and running models across NVIDIA, Apple Silicon, and AMD from one spec.

🔐 Routing and policy

Adding a ModelRouter enables policy-aware routing between local models and external providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and LiteLLM. A rule matching requests labeled pii/phi by header can route only to local-tier backends. Content detection is planned (#441).

🚀 Availability and maturity

LLMKube is Apache-2.0 licensed, actively developed, and intended to run across homelab and on-prem fleets. It is pre-1.0: every CRD is v1alpha1, and fields can change between minor releases. For running one model on one laptop, Ollama is simpler.

#Kubernetes #LLM #Inference #GPUs #OpenAIAPI

Source: defilantech/LLMKube

item.title: Open Model Engine Automates Kubernetes-Based LLM Serving
item.description:
Open Model Engine Automates Kubernetes-Based LLM Serving

Open Model Engine (OME) is a Kubernetes operator for enterprise-grade management and serving of large language models (LLMs), including model lifecycle management, GPU scheduling, and runtime selection.

🔍 Overview

OME treats models as first-class custom resources and supports more than 200 pre-configured models, including the Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma, and Phi families. It works with SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and Triton.

🧩 How it works

  • Model parsing extracts architecture, parameter count, and capabilities directly from model files.
  • OME matches models to runtime configurations using weighted scoring based on architecture, format, quantization, parameter size, and framework compatibility.
  • Distributed model storage supports automated repair, double encryption, namespace scoping, and SafeTensors, PyTorch, TensorRT, and ONNX formats.
  • AcceleratorClass resources define GPU capabilities, discovery patterns, and cost information. Policies can select accelerators using BestFit, Cheapest, or MostCapable criteria.
  • Specialized GPU bin-packing scheduling dynamically re-optimizes placements to improve cluster efficiency while ensuring high availability.

⚙️ Deployment and integrations

OME supports several deployment patterns and Kubernetes integrations:

  • Prefill-decode disaggregation, multi-node inference, and traditional Kubernetes deployments.
  • Canary and blue-green rollouts, along with advanced scaling controls.
  • Kueue for gang scheduling of multi-pod workloads, LeaderWorkerSet for resilient multi-node deployments, and KEDA for custom-metrics-based autoscaling.
  • Kubernetes Gateway API for traffic routing and Gateway API Inference Extension for standardized inference endpoints.
  • Optional add-on control planes for large GPU fleets. The quota manager assembles the AcceleratorQuota tree and renders it into Kueue.

OME provides first-class support for SGLang features including cache-aware load balancing, multi-node deployment, prefill-decode disaggregated serving, and multi-LoRA adapter serving. It also supports vLLM for high-throughput inference.

🛠️ Management and evaluation

  • The kubectl ome CLI plugin inspects models, runtimes, inference services, and logical instances. It explains runtime and accelerator selection and reports rollout, autoscaling, placement, quota, and traffic evidence.
  • The CLI can stream component logs and submit guarded actions, including rollout pause, resume, promote, and rollback; traffic drain; and migration requests.
  • A web interface manages models, serving runtimes, and inference services with real-time updates and HuggingFace model search integration.
  • The BenchmarkJob custom resource provides built-in performance evaluation.

🚀 Requirements and operations

  • Requires Kubernetes 1.28 or newer; API version: v1beta1.
  • Includes unit and integration test coverage and has production deployments with large-scale LLM workloads.
  • Monitoring uses standard metrics and Kubernetes events.
  • Security features include RBAC-based access control and model encryption.
  • High-availability mode includes redundant model storage.

The Qdrant Helm chart has been introduced, enabling users to deploy Qdrant within their Kubernetes clusters. While distributed deployment is possible, the chart lacks advanced features found in Qdrant Cloud and Private Cloud Enterprise Operator offerings.

item.title: NVIDIA Upstreams Agent Substrate and Introduces Snapshot, NVKE, and NVKR
item.description:
NVIDIA Upstreams Agent Substrate and Introduces Snapshot, NVKE, and NVKR

NVIDIA is contributing upstream to Agent Substrate—an open-source agent runtime donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox—while introducing NVIDIA Snapshot, NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE), and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) as part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform.

🔍 Overview

Agent Substrate, NVIDIA Snapshot, NVKE, and NVKR address infrastructure needs across AI agent session management, GPU workload startup times, and managed Kubernetes cluster operations.

Component Description Status / License
Agent Substrate Security-hardened runtime that multiplexes sandboxed agent sessions over worker Pods Donated to CNCF Sandbox
NVIDIA Snapshot Checkpoint and restore system for GPU workloads on Kubernetes Open-source (DSX AI Factory)
NVKE Software to run managed Kubernetes clusters on factory infrastructure Apache 2.0 (Public Preview)
NVKR Reproducible builds for OS images, container images, and Helm charts Apache 2.0 (Public Preview)

🧩 How Agent Substrate Works

Agent Substrate provides a security-hardened, zero-trust runtime engineered to run agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers by decoupling actor state from worker Pods:

  • Session Multiplexing: Idle sessions are snapshotted out of gVisor or microVM sandboxes—including memory and filesystem state—freeing the underlying worker Pod.
  • Bypassing Control Plane Latency: Restoring an actor onto a free worker Pod skips API server, admission, etcd, scheduler, and kubelet roundtrips.
  • Kubernetes Integration: Worker Pods remain standard Kubernetes Pods, ensuring cluster scheduling, placement policies, and quotas continue to apply.
  • Upstream Capabilities: Public developments include router request parking (#221), request line protection for running actors (#1229), and Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) device pluggability (#752), with NVIDIA GPUs designated as the first supported device.

⚡ NVIDIA Snapshot GPU Checkpoint and Restore

NVIDIA Snapshot eliminates repeated workload initialization by saving fully initialized CPU and GPU memory states into portable artifacts:

  • Operations: Checkpointing is managed via PodSnapshot or SnapshotJob custom resources, while restoration uses the nvidia.com/restore-from Pod annotation.
  • Workload Compatibility: Features examples for vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM, and supports single-node multi-GPU workloads across tensor parallelism (TP), data and expert parallelism (DEP), and decode context parallelism (DCP).
  • Restoration Speed: Across tested configurations, Snapshot restores replicas in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds—8x to 36x faster than cold starts. Crusoe reduced GLM-5.3 Pod readiness from ~8 minutes to 31 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300, while Saturn Cloud cut vLLM startup from 2–8.5 minutes to 6–34 seconds.

🛠️ NVKE and NVKR Infrastructure Tools

NVKE and NVKR allow AI factories to construct and operate managed Kubernetes services:

  • NVKR (NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes): Builds validated operating system images, container images, binaries, and Helm charts based on specific GPU generations and software versions.
  • NVKE (NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine): Deploys management and workload clusters using artifacts produced by NVKR, leveraging Cluster API infrastructure provider CAPNICo and NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo).
  • Node Identity & Observability: Requires nodes to present an attested SPIFFE identity before receiving join credentials, and exports telemetry via an OpenTelemetry-based Helm chart over OTLP.
  • Certification: NVKE is a Certified Kubernetes AI Platform and Certified Kubernetes Installer tested on Kubernetes 1.36.

item.title: NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform adds open‑source tools for reliable GPU‑Kubernetes clusters
item.description:
NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform adds open‑source tools for reliable GPU‑Kubernetes clusters

One underperforming GPU can slow an entire distributed training job, so measuring goodput – the volume of work successfully completed – is a more useful way to gauge cluster efficiency. NVIDIA’s DSX AI Factory Platform bundles the technologies needed to design, build, and operate efficient, resilient AI factories.

🔍 Overview

  • The platform’s open‑source software layer, NVIDIA DSX OS, provides tools for configuring, certifying, and maintaining the health of accelerated Kubernetes infrastructure.
  • It aims to keep every GPU, node, and network component in a ready state so that goodput remains high across large training jobs.

🛠️ Components

Component What it does
NVIDIA DSX OS Configures, certifies, and maintains accelerated Kubernetes clusters.
NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) Establishes a reproducible, version‑locked baseline for GPU‑optimized Kubernetes infrastructure; renders configuration recipes as bundles for existing deployment tools.
NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE) Validates cluster readiness for production workloads; tests GPUs, networking, and storage with AI workloads and diagnostics; records certification results and flags faulty nodes.
NVSentinel Monitors cluster health; publishes node conditions based on GPU, node, and network health; cordons or taints unhealthy nodes, drains workloads, remediates faults, and can trigger re‑validation with NVCRE before returning nodes to service.

All three projects are licensed under Apache 2.0 and welcome external contributions.

⚙️ How it works

  • AICR defines the cluster’s software baseline in version‑controlled files and renders them into artifacts that any deployment tool can apply.
  • Declarative templates detect configuration drift from manual changes and keep node configurations consistent after repairs.
  • Each recipe entry pins a component version, declares required healthy dependencies, and includes a healthCheckAsserts block that runs after installation.
  • The health assertions filter on the container waiting reason rather than the pod phase alone.
  • The bundle command produces ready‑to‑use artifacts: 
    1

    aicr bundle --recipe recipe.yaml --deployer argocd --output ./bundles
  • The --deployer flag accepts helm, argocd, argocd‑helm, flux, or helmfile, so the same validated recipe can become Argo CD Application manifests, Flux resources, a Helmfile release graph, or plain Helm commands.
  • Because the recipe is a file, standard version‑control workflows (history, code review, drift detection) manage the baseline.
  • Drift detection can be enforced as a CI gate: 
    1

    aicr diff --baseline ./golden.yaml --target cm://default/aicr-snapshot --fail-on-drift

📊 Measuring Efficiency

  • Goodput focuses on the actual work completed, highlighting the impact of any slow GPU on overall training performance.

🚀 Availability

  • The DSX OS, AICR, NVCRE, and NVSentinel projects are all open source under the Apache 2.0 license.
  • External contributions are encouraged, and the tools integrate with common GitOps deployment pipelines.

#NVIDIA #Kubernetes #AIInfrastructure #GPUClusters

item.title: NVIDIA Launches Workload Map to Standardize Distributed AI Workloads on Kubernetes
item.description:
NVIDIA Launches Workload Map to Standardize Distributed AI Workloads on Kubernetes

NVIDIA has introduced Workload Map as part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, providing a common description for Kubernetes workload structures to help the ecosystem design, build, and operate more efficient AI factories.

🔍 Overview

Operating an AI factory requires a shared understanding of distributed workloads, including their pod templates, replica counts, and status. Currently, each framework on Kubernetes encodes this information differently. Distributed training jobs or multi-node inference servers are often structured as trees of resources where groups of pods have specific roles and statuses. Until now, tools like schedulers, dashboards, and controllers required separate, framework-specific adapters to interpret these various custom resources.

🧩 How it works

Workload Map (formerly known as Karta) consists of a Kubernetes CRD and a Go library that resolves live objects into a uniform structural view. Instead of maintaining separate parsing code for every framework, developers can describe a workload type once using a YAML definition. This definition specifies where to find pod templates, replica counts, and status fields.

Key features include:

  • Shared Structural View: Supplies a common description that can be reused across different frameworks and tools.
  • Data-Driven Logic: Moves workload knowledge out of compiled adapters and into data manifests that can be reviewed and applied to a cluster.
  • Reduced Development Time: Eliminates the need to wait for platform releases to support new workload types, as users can add support by writing a new YAML definition.

⚙️ Key details

Workload Map enables integrated platforms to interpret supported workload types without separate parsing code. For example, the KAI Scheduler uses these definitions for pod grouping and gang-scheduling instructions, while NVIDIA Run:ai utilizes them for workload management and visibility.

Feature Description
Resource Kind Karta (CRD)
Components Kubernetes CRD and a Go library
Platform Integration NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, KAI Scheduler, and NVIDIA Run:ai
Management Supports multi-tenant operations and scaling

📋 Supported Frameworks

Workload Map includes a catalog of prebuilt and tested definitions for a variety of frameworks and services, including:

  • Training & Batch: JobSet, PyTorchJob, MPIJob, and LeaderWorkerSet.
  • Orchestration & Services: RayCluster, RayJob, RayService, KServe, and Knative.
  • Specialized Tools: NVIDIA NIM, Milvus, Grove PodCliqueSet, and NVIDIA Dynamo.

💡 Why it matters

Previously, supporting a new framework was a roadmap item that required a per-CRD adapter. For instance, a JobSet manifest describing a leader job and two worker jobs (totaling 12 GPUs) would typically require JobSet-aware code to aggregate resource requests. By using Workload Map, teams building schedulers, controllers, or cost tools can interpret these complex distributed workloads through a single, shared definition, reducing the ongoing cost of adapter development.

item.title: NVIDIA releases Dynamo 1.4.2 with AICR‑packaged recipes for Kubernetes inference
item.description:
NVIDIA releases Dynamo 1.4.2 with AICR‑packaged recipes for Kubernetes inference

NVIDIA has updated its Dynamo distributed inference framework to version 1.4.2 and delivered it through the NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) as validated recipes that simplify deployment on Kubernetes.

🔍 Overview

  • Dynamo is a distributed inference framework that coordinates model serving across GPU workers.
  • It is part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, which helps the ecosystem design, build, and operate more efficient AI factories.
  • AICR (AI Cluster Runtime) packages Dynamo and its supporting infrastructure into reproducible recipes.

🧩 How it works

  • Running a model with Dynamo on Kubernetes begins with a DynamoGraphDeployment custom resource that specifies how vLLM, SGLang, or NVIDIA TensorRT LLM should run in pods.
  • Frontends, workers, and optional Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE) / Endpoint Picker Plugin (EPP) components discover each other through Kubernetes resources.
  • Dynamo routes requests to workers that already hold the relevant KV‑cache blocks via its frontend router or through GAIE/EPP integration at the Gateway API layer.
  • The framework can separate prompt processing (prefill) from token generation (decode), a pattern called disaggregated serving. On KV‑cache misses the prefill pool reprocesses the prompt, after which decode workers generate tokens token‑by‑token.
  • In Dynamo 1.4.2 the default AICR Kubernetes path uses TCP for the request plane and ZMQ for KV‑cache events. Each vLLM worker emits raw KV‑cache events through a local ZMQ publisher.

⚙️ Key details

  • AICR ships version 1.4.2 of the dynamo‑platform chart, which includes the Dynamo operator, runtime images, and the nvidia.com/v1beta1 DynamoGraphDeployment CRD (replacing the former v1alpha1).
  • The AICR Dynamo recipe pins component versions and records configuration values, node selectors, tolerations, checksums, and validation expectations to make deployment reproducible.
  • The default path no longer installs NATS; it remains available as an opt‑in for deployments that need it.
Component Role / Note
DynamoGraphDeployment CRD (v1beta1) Defines deployment of vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT LLM pods
dynamo‑platform chart 1.4.2 Packages Dynamo operator, runtime images, and related resources
AICR Dynamo recipe Pins versions, records config, node selectors, tolerations, checksums, validation expectations
GAIE / EPP (optional) Provides Gateway API routing integration
NATS (optional) Message bus that is not installed by default

🚀 Availability

  • The AICR distribution includes the 1.4.2 chart and the associated validated recipe.
  • Support for vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM is built into the DynamoGraphDeployment specification.
  • Operators can choose between the default TCP + ZMQ transport or opt‑in to NATS if required.

💡 Why it matters

  • AICR gives platform teams a repeatable way to deploy and validate the runtime, providing developers with a consistent foundation for serving models and testing applications.
  • Disaggregated serving lets operators scale and tune prefill and decode capacity independently, accommodating different request mixes such as long‑running agentic sessions versus one‑off chat requests.
  • By routing requests to workers that already hold the needed KV‑cache blocks, Dynamo reduces the need to reprocess intermediate tokens on cache misses.

item.title: AWS releases Ray Train Deep Learning Container for distributed PyTorch training
item.description:
AWS releases Ray Train Deep Learning Container for distributed PyTorch training

AWS has released the Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC), a pre-integrated software stack designed to simplify distributed machine learning training. The image is built, tested as a single unit, and maintained by AWS to ensure compatibility across the various libraries required for multi-node workloads.

🔍 Overview

The Ray Train DLC is a PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries layered on top. It includes the full HuggingFace training stack, allowing users to run fine-tuning jobs without building or pushing new images. AWS publishes these images to the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public, where they can be pulled without credentials.

Component Function
CUDA Runtime Provides the foundational environment for GPU acceleration.
PyTorch Compiled against the specific CUDA runtime in the image.
NCCL NVIDIA Collective Communications Library for GPU communication.
EFA Libraries Userspace libraries for the Elastic Fabric Adapter.
AWS OFI NCCL Plugin Connects NCCL to EFA for high-performance networking.
Ray Coordinates the cluster and manages training libraries.

🧩 How it works

Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two distinct roles, both of which use the same tagged image. Whether running on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) via KubeRay or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), the container’s role is determined by the startup command.

  • Ray Head: Coordinates the cluster, tracks state in the global control store, and runs the dashboard and job server.
  • Ray Worker: Supplies GPUs and executes the training processes, connecting to the head’s address at startup.

On Kubernetes, the KubeRay operator adds a RayCluster resource that builds and maintains these groups from a single manifest.

⚙️ Key details

The Ray Train DLC is designed to be configured entirely from outside the image. Users specify instance types, GPU counts, and network transport settings through external configuration files rather than by modifying the container.

  • Compatibility: The image entrypoint automatically enables bundled CUDA forward-compatibility libraries if the host’s NVIDIA driver is older than the image’s CUDA version.
  • Performance: Collective operations between instances run over EFA automatically as soon as pods request it, as the EFA stack is pre-installed.
  • Testing: AWS gates each release on multi-node EFA and multi-node KubeRay training tests.

🚀 Availability

The Ray Train DLC is available in the Amazon ECR repository under the train-ml tag prefix, sharing a repository with Ray Serve and Ray LLM DLCs.

A provided sample demonstrates the DLC’s capabilities by fine-tuning a Qwen2.5-1.5B model using PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances.

item.title: GPU Fractioning Operator Enables Fine‑Grained GPU Sharing in Kubernetes
item.description:
GPU Fractioning Operator Enables Fine‑Grained GPU Sharing in Kubernetes

Many AI workloads need only a fraction of a GPU, and allocating a whole device to each workload can leave capacity idle. An open‑source Kubernetes operator called gpu‑fractioning now lets platform teams share GPUs at the memory and compute level, using new CUDA 13.4 enforcement features and NVIDIA’s existing sharing mechanisms.

🔍 Overview

  • AI workloads often require only part of a GPU’s memory and compute resources.
  • Sharing GPUs lets platform teams serve more workloads with the same hardware.
  • NVIDIA GPUs already support several sharing approaches: MIG, time‑slicing, and Multi‑Process Service (MPS).

🛠️ How it works

  • CUDA 13.4 memory enforcement: a workload requests a memory size; CUDA reserves it and rejects allocations that exceed the limit, giving the workload a guaranteed minimum and a maximum it can grow into when memory is free.
  • Compute modes: each workload can run in the default time‑sharing mode or choose the sm‑sharing mode (MPS) that runs processes concurrently in separate address spaces.
  • The enforcement logic runs on the node; it is independent of the scheduler that placed the workload.

⚙️ Key components

  • gpu‑fractioning operator (hosted under the KAI Scheduler GitHub organization) – sets up MPS on every GPU node, applies per‑workload memory limits and compute mode, and measures usage per fraction.
  • NVIDIA GPU Operator – provides the driver and container‑runtime setup; gpu‑fractioning runs alongside it.
  • Pod annotations – developers specify resource limits and compute mode in the pod YAML; the scheduler writes the chosen GPU slice and mode into per‑container annotations.
  • GPU Fractioning Operator – reads those annotations and configures the assigned GPUs to enforce the requested memory and compute settings.
  • KAI Scheduler – first scheduler integrated with gpu‑fractioning; from version v0.18.0 it offers a sharing mode called NvFractions that selects a slice of a GPU for each workload and writes the required annotations.

🚀 Availability

  • The gpu‑fractioning operator is open source and lives on GitHub under the KAI Scheduler organization.
  • It works with any Kubernetes scheduler capable of writing the required annotations; KAI Scheduler is the reference implementation.
  • Starting with KAI Scheduler v0.18.0, the NvFractions mode is available out‑of‑the‑box.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables multiple AI workloads to run on a single GPU without idle capacity.
  • Provides transparent memory enforcement and optional compute sharing modes.
  • Allows administrators to choose the sharing strategy that best fits their cluster.

GPU sharing techniques in NVIDIA GPUs

Technique Key property
Multi‑Instance GPU (MIG) Splits a GPU into hardware‑isolated instances that are transparent to the application
Time‑slicing Lets several processes take turns without memory enforcement
Multi‑Process Service (MPS) – sm‑sharing Runs processes concurrently in separate address spaces

#GPUSharing #Kubernetes #CUDA #AIWorkloads

item.title: Multi-Node LLM Inference on Amazon EKS with Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
item.description:
Multi-Node LLM Inference on Amazon EKS with Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers

This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the multi‑node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers. The deployment separates the prefill and decode phases onto distinct GPU workers behind a single OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.

🔍 Overview

  • Ray is a distributed compute framework; Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes.
  • AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) are pre‑built, performance‑optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately.
  • The new Ray LLM DLC extends this approach to multi‑node inference.

🏗️ Architecture

  • CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) runs system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head pod (CPU‑only).
  • Two GPU worker nodes (g6.8xlarge) run Ray workers: one dedicated to the prefill phase, the other to the decode phase.
  • Both GPU nodes pull the Ray LLM DLC from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR).
  • KubeRay watches the RayService you apply and automatically wires the head‑to‑worker join.
  • Ray Serve places the prefill and decode deployments on the two GPU workers.
  • KV‑cache generated by prefill is transferred to the decode worker over NIXL, using the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) through NIXL’s libfabric backend.

⚙️ How It Works

  • Prefill phase
    • Processes the entire input prompt in parallel.
    • Builds the key‑value (KV) cache.
    • Compute‑bound.
  • Decode phase
    • Generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending the KV cache.
    • Memory‑bandwidth‑bound.
  • Separating the phases prevents compute‑heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress.
  • Disaggregation allows each phase to use hardware and serving properties tuned to its workload, improving overall performance at scale.
  • The trade‑off is that the KV cache must be handed from prefill to decode quickly enough to retain the benefit.

📦 Key Components

Component Role
Ray LLM DLC Packages Ray Serve LLM, NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL), and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack; exposes an OpenAI‑compatible API with no application code
vLLM Inference engine
Ray Serve HTTP Serving layer
NIXL KV‑cache transfer between nodes
EFA stack (libfabric, aws‑ofi‑nccl) High‑bandwidth node‑to‑node communication
AWS Deep Learning Containers Pre‑built, performance‑optimized Docker images ensuring no version drift between CUDA runtime, framework, and serving layer

🚀 Deployment Details

  • The Ray LLM DLC ships Ray Serve LLM, NIXL, and the EFA stack, ready for multi‑node inference.
  • No application code is required to expose the OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.
  • This multi‑node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as for prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads.
  • In a previous post, the Ray Serve DLC was used to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node.

💡 Why It Matters

  • By assigning prefill and decode to separate GPUs, compute‑heavy prefill work no longer contends with latency‑sensitive decode work.
  • Independent scaling of each phase enables better resource utilization and lower latency for LLM serving at scale.
  • All components are validated together before each release, guaranteeing compatibility across the CUDA runtime, framework, and serving layer.

#AWS #Ray #LLM #Kubernetes #Inference

Source: Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod adds multi‑tenant EKS support with Identity Center integration
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod adds multi‑tenant EKS support with Identity Center integration

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports purpose‑built, multi‑tenant AI clusters that simplify the management of large‑scale gen‑AI workloads while providing per‑team isolation, cost visibility, and automated operations.

🔍 Overview

  • HyperPod delivers resilient, optimized clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) or Slurm.
  • The service automatically handles node health monitoring, fault recovery, and cluster lifecycle management.
  • It is designed for distributed training, interactive development, and model inference at scale.

🧩 Architecture Overview

  • AWS IAM Identity Center provides centralized authentication and federates with external providers such as Microsoft Entra ID.
  • Each team gets a dedicated SageMaker AI domain that hosts a private SageMaker Studio GUI.
  • Workloads run in separate Kubernetes namespaces, ensuring isolation.
  • HyperPod Task Governance enforces fair resource allocation and compute‑quota management.
  • HyperPod Observability supplies monitoring dashboards for the entire cluster.
  • Storage is split into two tiers:
    • A POSIX‑compliant file system (Amazon FSx for Lustre or OpenZFS) with per‑team shared directories (/fsx/TeamA, /fsx/TeamB) and per‑user home directories (/home/User1, /home/User2).
    • Per‑team or shared Amazon S3 buckets governed by the team’s IAM execution role.

⚙️ Key Details

Component Role
AWS IAM Identity Center Centralized authentication; federates with external IdP; provisions permission‑set roles (e.g., TeamA-permissionset-role).
SageMaker AI domain (per team) Dedicated Studio GUI; uses team‑specific execution role (e.g., TeamA-role).
Kubernetes namespace (per team) Isolates workloads; scoped RBAC policies restrict access to the team’s resources.
HyperPod Task Governance Provides compute‑quota management and scheduling priorities across teams.
HyperPod Observability Offers monitoring dashboards and health metrics for the cluster.

Authentication Paths

  • CLI path: Users run aws sso login, are redirected to the Identity Center portal, obtain temporary credentials from their team’s permission set, and submit tasks to the EKS cluster with kubectl using the provisioned TeamA-permissionset-role or TeamB-permissionset-role.
  • Studio path: Users select the SageMaker Studio application in the Identity Center portal, which routes them to their team‑specific SageMaker AI domain. The domain’s execution role (TeamA-role or TeamB-role) authorizes GUI‑driven tasks.
  • Access entries map both the Studio execution roles and the CLI/Console roles to Kubernetes permissions, all tied to managed or custom RBAC policies scoped to the appropriate namespace.

🚀 Usage Example

  • Two teams, Team A and Team B, share a single HyperPod EKS cluster.
  • Each team operates within its own isolated namespace (Namespace A, Namespace B).
  • Within a namespace, teams can launch:
    • HyperPod Spaces – interactive development environments.
    • HyperPod PyTorch jobs – distributed training workloads.
    • HyperPod Inference endpoints – model serving services.
  • Cost allocation is performed at the namespace level, giving each team visibility into spend and supporting charge‑back.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a single, managed compute platform that reduces the operational overhead of large‑scale AI workloads.
  • Guarantees workload isolation and security through namespace‑scoped RBAC and distinct IAM roles.
  • Enables per‑team cost tracking and fair resource distribution via Task Governance.
  • Integrates with existing AWS identity and storage services, allowing teams to use familiar tools (CLI, SageMaker Studio) without custom configuration.

item.title: Microsoft Research Asia releases Harnessed Agentic RL with Agent Lightning v1.0
item.description:
Microsoft Research Asia releases Harnessed Agentic RL with Agent Lightning v1.0

Microsoft Research Asia introduced the Harnessed Agentic RL training paradigm and open‑sourced Agent Lightning v1.0, a lightweight framework that lets the same agent harness used in deployment participate directly in reinforcement learning.

🔍 Overview

  • Harnessed Agentic RL removes the need to reimplement the agent inside the training framework.
  • Agent Lightning v1.0 provides a complete agent RL control plane in roughly 3,500 lines of code.
  • The framework runs agents as standard Kubernetes jobs on self‑managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure, without reliance on paid commercial sandbox services.

🧩 How it works

  • The agent continues to call the model through an LLM proxy; the training system only observes the request‑response pairs.
  • The agent harness that coordinates the deployed agent also handles the environment interaction loop during training.
  • Because only LLM calls are recorded, a single rollout can be split into a variable number of training samples.
  • Retokenization is required to obtain token IDs; re‑tokenizing text can shift token boundaries, so adjacent calls may not be merged into one sample.

⚙️ Key details

  • Lightweight design – the entire codebase is about 3,500 lines, making it easy to understand, modify, and extend.
  • Native Kubernetes support – agents run directly as Kubernetes jobs, supporting self‑managed, cloud, and local clusters.
  • Data‑efficient training recipe – an end‑to‑end coding‑agent pipeline raised Qwen3.5‑9B from 41.8 % to 56.4 % Pass@1 on SWE‑bench Verified, a 14.6 percentage‑point gain using only ≈6,000 training samples from an open‑sourced dataset.
  • Traditional vs. harnessed RL – conventional agentic RL assumes the training framework owns the interaction loop, requiring developers to rebuild the agent’s context management, tool protocols, and execution logic inside the RL framework. This rebuilding is costly and can produce a training agent that differs from the deployed agent.

📊 Early systems and agents

AReaL Early RL system built with training framework owning the loop

🚀 Availability

  • The researchers released Agent Lightning v1.0 as an open‑source project.
  • v1.0 emphasizes staying lightweight, integrating with real harnesses, and providing a reproducible agent RL training pipeline.
  • By pointing the endpoint that previously called the model API at Agent Lightning, developers can train using the same harness that will be deployed.

💡 Why it matters

item.title: NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime v1.0 delivers version‑locked GPU‑Kubernetes recipes
item.description:
NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime v1.0 delivers version‑locked GPU‑Kubernetes recipes

NVIDIA released version 1.0 of the AI Cluster Runtime (AICR), a library of version‑locked, validated recipes that simplify the configuration of GPU‑accelerated Kubernetes clusters.

🔍 Overview

  • GPU‑accelerated Kubernetes clusters depend on compatible versions across dozens of components, each on its own release cycle: host kernels, GPU drivers, container runtimes, networking, storage, operators, and workload frameworks.
  • A configuration that works for one service, GPU generation, and Kubernetes release may silently fail for another, and tracing version conflicts after deployment is slow and error‑prone.
  • AICR addresses this with version‑locked, validated recipes for GPU cluster configuration.

🧩 How it works

AICR element Purpose
Recipe Describes the desired, version‑locked component configuration and the constraints and validation phases that apply to it.
Bundle Renders the recipe into deployment artifacts for Helm, Argo CD, Flux, or Helmfile (or other IaC tools).
Snapshot Records observed cluster state, including Kubernetes, operating system, kernel, GPU, and topology information.
Validation Compares the recipe with observed state and, where declared, runs deployment, conformance, and performance checks; records signed evidence of the result.

The workflow is:

  1. Operator selects criteria (e.g., service, GPU, OS, workload intent) on the validation dashboard.
  2. The dashboard resolves those criteria to a pinned recipe.
  3. The recipe is rendered as a bundle for the operator’s preferred deployment tool (Argo CD, Helm, Flux, Helmfile, etc.).
  4. The bundle is applied to the cluster using the chosen CD tool.
  5. AICR validates the running cluster against the same recipe and stores signed evidence.

⚙️ Key details

  • All recipes are version‑locked and carry signed validation evidence from the hardware they were tested on.
  • v1.0 establishes a stable compatibility contract across its CLI, REST API, Go SDK, bundle layout, and artifact schemas.
  • The v1.x compatibility policy allows integrators to build against AICR’s public interfaces.
  • Contributors can propose recipes, validate them on their own clusters, and submit signed evidence for maintainer review.
  • Recent additions include live‑cluster validation, signed evidence, public evidence aggregation, and supply‑chain verification.
  • Merge‑blocking checks and committed compatibility baselines protect the public integration surfaces.
  • Pulumi Labs exposes AICR through an infrastructure‑as‑code provider, while Mirantis’s k0rdent integration packages it for multi‑cluster management.
  • Together they demonstrate the value of defining GPU‑accelerated Kubernetes configuration once and consuming it through different tools.

🚀 Availability

  • v1.0 is the first stable release of AICR.
  • Over the past six months the library grew from a handful of recipes to a collection spanning major Kubernetes services and the current NVIDIA accelerator portfolio, rendered as deployer‑neutral bundles.
  • AICR now has over 100 distinct contributors, with almost half from outside of NVIDIA.

💡 Why it matters

  • Prevents silent failures caused by hidden version mismatches across components.
  • Centralises knowledge of working component combinations that previously lived in separate validation systems, deployment scripts, and runbooks.
  • Enables teams to discover, reproduce, and update working configurations through a single dashboard and a unified set of public interfaces.
  • Provides signed evidence and supply‑chain verification, increasing trust in the deployed cluster configuration.
  • Allows operators to keep their existing GitOps or IaC workflows (Helm, Argo CD, Flux, Helmfile) while guaranteeing the intended configuration does not change across tooling.

#NVIDIA #Kubernetes #GPU #AICR

item.title: Accelerating Mixture-of-Experts Training with Amazon EKS, EFA, and DeepEP
item.description:
Accelerating Mixture-of-Experts Training with Amazon EKS, EFA, and DeepEP

AWS has described an architecture optimized to accelerate the training of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, specifically addressing the infrastructure challenges associated with large-scale Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training.

🔍 Overview

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a standard architecture for scaling large language models (LLMs) to hundreds of billions or trillions of parameters while maintaining efficient inference through sparsity. However, large-scale RL training—including pipelines based on Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)—places unusual demands on infrastructure. These demands arise because RL combines elastic inference work with tightly coupled model training that requires high-bandwidth communication.

⚙️ Key Details

Large-scale asynchronous RL jobs must optimize two distinct, simultaneous workloads:

  • Rollout Generation: Distributed inference focused on maximizing aggregate throughput rather than minimizing inter-token latency or time to first token (TTFT).
  • Policy Training: Tightly coupled workers that progress in lockstep; any straggling worker or latency spike can trigger NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) timeouts or stall the entire job.

Training MoE models introduces specific constraints compared to dense models. As architectures become more sparse to reduce inference costs, training is constrained more by communication than by compute. A primary source of this overhead is Expert Parallelism (EP), which introduces dynamic all-to-all token routing across devices in addition to standard Tensor Parallelism (TP), Data Parallelism (DP), and Pipeline Parallelism (PP).

🧩 How it works

To address these challenges, an architecture combining the following tools is used:

Component Purpose
Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Orchestrates large-scale RL training and coordinates heterogeneous compute.
Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) Accelerates large-scale RL training and provides high-bandwidth inter-node communication.
DeepEP Optimizes expert-parallel communication over EFA.

This system must balance three resource constraints to prevent bottlenecks or idle capacity:

  • Accelerator compute
  • Memory (including KV-cache capacity for distributed inference)
  • Network bandwidth

#AWS #MoE #ReinforcementLearning #LLM #Kubernetes

item.description:
NVIDIA Open Sources NodeWright for Kubernetes Host Infrastructure Management

NVIDIA has released NodeWright as an open-source, Kubernetes-native package manager designed to modify and maintain host infrastructure at scale. As part of the NVIDIA DSX OS open-source software layer, NodeWright enables the declarative configuration and safe updating of Kubernetes node operating systems without disrupting workloads.

🔍 Overview

NodeWright is a component of the NVIDIA DSX platform, which treats entire facilities as single systems (AI factories) rather than collections of machines. It is part of the supporting infrastructure capabilities that include:

  • NVIDIA GPU Operator
  • NVIDIA Network Operator
  • Topograph
  • DRA Driver for NVIDIA GPUs
  • NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE)
  • NVSentinel

🧩 How it works

NodeWright consists of three main components:

Component Description
Operator A Kubernetes controller that watches for custom resources and manages the lifecycle of changes across nodes.
Custom Resources Used to define NodeWright packages; these deploy via tools such as kubectl, Helm, Argo CD, or Flux.
Packages Container images containing binaries, configurations, scripts, and verification scripts to surface failures and stop incorrect rollouts.

When applying changes, NodeWright follows a specific operational flow:

  1. Cordon: Marks the node as unschedulable.
  2. Wait: Allows critical workloads to finish gracefully.
  3. Drain: Evicts remaining pods, honoring PodDisruptionBudgets by default.
  4. Apply and configure: Runs the package to set kernel parameters, install agents, and configure system services.
  5. Interrupt: Restarts a service or reboots the node if required.
  6. Uncordon: Returns the node to the cluster for workloads.

⚙️ Key details

NodeWright manages the full lifecycle of host-level changes, including installation, configuration, upgrade, and uninstallation. Key capabilities include:

  • Infrastructure Operations: Performs tasks that normally require root access without recycling nodes, such as setting sysctl and GRUB parameters, configuring crash dump collection, creating logical volumes, installing security agents, and remediating CVEs.
  • Workload Awareness: Respects Kubernetes primitives including node selectors, taints, tolerations, and PodDisruptionBudgets.
  • State Tracking: Tracks the semantic version and state of every package on every node to distinguish between fresh installations, upgrades, and downgrades.
  • Dependency Management: Uses declared dependencies to determine the correct execution order.

🚀 Availability

NodeWright is available as open source and has run in production at NVIDIA under the name Skyhook.

item.title: NVIDIA Releases Open Source Cluster Readiness Engine for Kubernetes
item.description:
NVIDIA Releases Open Source Cluster Readiness Engine for Kubernetes

NVIDIA has introduced the Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE), an open source Kubernetes controller designed to identify hardware and configuration issues in GPU clusters before production workloads are deployed.

💡 Why it matters

Standard diagnostics can report that every GPU, network link, and pod is healthy, yet a 512-GPU training job may still underperform or fail. Potential causes include:

  • A single slow GPU.
  • A link that degrades under load.
  • A configuration that routes traffic over a slower path.

Without specialized tooling, operators may only discover these problems hours into a run or via customer tickets, leading to days of manual cluster bisection while capacity remains idle. NVCRE transforms readiness from an assumption into a proven property by running real distributed workloads that expose hardware problems.

⚙️ Key details

On Slurm, testing readiness requires a single srun command, but Kubernetes lacks a built-in equivalent. Running such tests on Kubernetes typically requires manual GPU and RDMA resource requests, NCCL settings matched to the network fabric, large shared-memory volumes, and mechanisms to ensure pods start together. NVCRE fills these gaps, removing the need for operators to:

  • Write NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) manifests by hand.
  • Bisect racks manually.
  • Rely on customer tickets to learn about degraded hardware.

NVCRE supports a staged readiness process where clusters move through bring-up, burn-in, preproduction, and production, with each stage setting a different bar. This replaces the need for platform teams to maintain custom runbooks, spreadsheets, or shell scripts wrapped around NCCL tests.

🧩 How it works

NVCRE uses an API based on Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs), allowing management through GitOps workflows and inspection via kubectl. The system uses a three-resource hierarchy to attribute failures to specific nodes and categories:

Resource Function
Certification The top-level resource that names the nodes to test and the categories to run.
Workflow Manages one category; applies overrides, manages iteration count, sets the orchestration target, and creates the child job.
Job Runs the workload for the target node group, monitors health, and records measurements and failures.

Results propagate upward from the Job to the Workflow and finally to the Certification. This allows the system to name exactly which node caused a failure, such as reporting that one GPU hit a hardware fault during NCCL while another missed its bandwidth target.

#NVIDIA #Kubernetes #GPU #OpenSource #ClusterManagement

Source: Validate GPU Cluster Readiness Before AI Workloads Land | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.description:
NVIDIA Releases Topograph Open Source Toolkit for Topology-Aware GPU Scheduling

NVIDIA has introduced Topograph, an open source toolkit designed to identify cluster network topology to enable workload managers to make topology-aware scheduling decisions.

💡 Why it matters

AI factories are power-limited systems that require full optimization to deliver maximum value. Because GPUs exchange data continuously during training and inference, distributed workloads benefit from communication locality. Poor workload placement can lead to:

  • Fragmented topology domains
  • Increased traffic across shared links
  • Reduced throughput and higher job costs
  • GPUs consuming provisioned power while waiting for data without advancing the workload

Topograph prevents these bottlenecks by mapping how cluster hardware is connected, allowing schedulers to favor nearby resources and avoid spreading tightly coupled workloads across distant domains.

🧩 How it works

Topograph solves the problem of maintaining an accurate view of GPU and fabric relationships as a cluster changes. It uses two primary concepts:

  • Providers: These discover topology from cloud APIs or on-premises systems and normalize it into a canonical model.
  • Engines: These translate the normalized model into formats expected by various workload managers.

Within the NVIDIA DSX OS cluster orchestration layer, Topograph works alongside KAI Scheduler and Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) to enable topology-aware gang scheduling.

⚙️ Key details

Topograph supports a variety of hardware and software integrations to ensure the scheduler works from current data rather than a manually maintained snapshot.

Component Supported Integration/Requirement
Cloud Providers Google Cloud, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale, and OCI
On-Premises Providers InfiniBand (with ibnetdiscover), NetQ (for Spectrum-X or Multi-Node NVLink domains)
Engines/Outputs Kubernetes node labels, Slurm topology configuration, Slinky ConfigMaps, Node Feature Discovery (NFD) resources, instance-oriented topology JSON
Slurm Engine Requires a writable volume for its configured topology.conf output path
NFD Engine Requires the alpha NodeFeatureGroupAPI feature gate
Crusoe Provider Runs in Kubernetes; reads fabric and accelerator-domain labels from Crusoe Managed Kubernetes nodes

🚀 Availability

Topograph is an open source toolkit with an open provider interface, allowing operators to add and contribute providers for their own environments upstream. item.title: Offloading Physical AI Inference to Edge and Cloud GPUs Improves Robot Performance

Offloading Physical AI Inference to Edge and Cloud GPUs Improves Robot Performance

Research indicates that offloading physical AI inference from onboard GPUs to edge or cloud infrastructure can enhance robot performance, battery life, and scalability compared to the prevailing approach of wiring GPUs directly to robots.

💡 Why it matters

Running AI inference exclusively on onboard GPUs introduces several limitations:

  • Power and Weight: GPUs consume significant power, add cost and weight, and can reduce battery life.
  • Hardware Constraints: Some smaller GPUs cannot accommodate the mobile manipulation stack, and onboard GPUs can limit the ability to run the latest generation of AI models.
  • Performance Drops: On GPUs with sufficient memory, mapping and planning slowed by up to 383% compared to an A100. Lighter GPUs caused a 30% drop in timely obstacle detection for navigation and a 50% drop in accuracy for VLA models.
  • Battery Drain: Larger onboard GPUs, such as Jetson Thor, drained robot batteries by up to 160% (or a few hours) for larger robots.

⚙️ Key details

The research focused on mobile robotic manipulation, using canonical tasks such as checking for rubbish in a kitchen and putting it in the trash. The evaluation covered three core capabilities:

Capability Impact of Offloading
Semantic mapping and planning Improved response time and accuracy; reduced slowdowns compared to onboard GPUs
Navigation Improved timely detection of obstacles
Manipulation Improved task success rates and accuracy

Replacing power-hungry onboard compute with lightweight hardware, such as a Raspberry Pi-5 board, and shipping data to an offloaded GPU substantially improves battery lifetime.

🧩 How it works

A new toolset has been developed to facilitate the distribution of inference between the robot, edge GPUs, and the cloud:

  • Orchestration: Uses Kubernetes-based tooling to provide a uniform abstraction for distributing robotic AI workloads.
  • Deployment: Allows for automatic containerization and offloading using declarative specifications and smart policies.
  • Integration: The toolset integrates with ROS2, LeRobot, and robotic simulators for development.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway for GPU-Aware Routing
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway for GPU-Aware Routing

Amazon has announced the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway, a Kubernetes-native, GPU-aware routing system designed to optimize how inference requests are placed on GPU clusters.

💡 Why it matters

Running large language models (LLMs) at scale on GPU clusters is expensive, and default Kubernetes load balancers can exacerbate this. Standard round-robin and least-connections algorithms lack visibility into GPU internals, such as:

  • Saturated KV caches
  • Long-context generations in progress
  • Loaded LoRA adapters in memory

These limitations cause requests to pile up behind busy pods while idle capacity remains unused, leading to unpredictable GPU utilization, wasted spend, and first-token latency spikes of 4+ seconds during traffic bursts.

🧩 How it works

The Inference Gateway uses a two-tier design built on Kubernetes-native primitives:

Tier Deployment Function
Tier 1 amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-inference addon Installs on each HyperPod/EKS cluster to handle local intelligent routing using real-time GPU signals.
Tier 2 Built on top of Tier 1 Provides fleet-wide coordination across multiple clusters and regions, including global rate limiting, cost-aware traffic shaping, and cross-cluster failover.

⚙️ Key details

  • Deployment: Deploys as a single EKS managed addon on existing HyperPod infrastructure using a declarative InferenceGatewayConfig custom resource.
  • Compatibility: Exposes a standard OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
  • Request Routing: The Body-Based Router natively routes requests to the correct model pool based on the model field in the request body via defined schedulers.
  • LoRA Optimization: The EPP’s LoRA Affinity Scorer identifies pods with the requested adapter resident in GPU memory to eliminate adapter swap latency. If no pod has it loaded, the request is routed to the pod with the most available capacity to load it quickly.
  • Tuning: Each scorer includes a configurable weight to tune routing for specific workloads, such as throughput-optimized batch or latency-sensitive chat.

Source: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway | Amazon Web Services

item.title: HyperPod InstantStart launched to simplify Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster composition
item.description:
HyperPod InstantStart launched to simplify Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster composition

Running foundation model (FM) workloads on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is a chain of dependent tasks rather than a single action. Infrastructure teams must create the network and control plane, attach accelerator capacity, install cluster dependencies, prepare storage and identity, and deploy model servers. To address the operational challenges of managing these handoffs, HyperPod InstantStart has been introduced as an open-source control plane built for resource composition.

🔍 Overview

While Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) provides direct Kubernetes access as a user-managed orchestration surface, it traditionally requires teams to compose AWS resources, add-ons, workloads, and day-two operations manually. Each step has its own API, failure modes, and waiting periods.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod reduces this operational burden by offering managed, resilient compute and Amazon EKS integrated capabilities. HyperPod InstantStart directly resolves the remaining composition challenges by automating multi-stage workflows.

🧩 How it works

HyperPod InstantStart runs as a single, out-of-band management container in your AWS account. It calls AWS service APIs and the Kubernetes API, but does not sit in the data path of your training jobs or inference requests.

The control plane offers two ways to drive its operations, both entering through the same single container:

  • AI Agent Orchestration: An AI agent plans the multi-stage workflow, launches each stage, and polls asynchronous AWS operations until completion. The agent pauses only for user-defined decisions—such as selecting the Availability Zone, instance type, and capacity type—before handing back a running cluster with storage mounted.
  • Unified Interfaces: The web UI, the REST API, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools represent three faces of the same container. Both interfaces call the same backend APIs, pass the same validations, and read the same persisted operation state, ensuring neither interface has private logic the other lacks.

Because everything created by HyperPod InstantStart is a standard AWS or Kubernetes resource, infrastructure teams can inspect all outputs directly using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and kubectl.

⚙️ Key details

The capabilities managed across AWS and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod are structured as follows:

Operational Category Managed Capabilities
Infrastructure Health monitoring, deep health checks, and automatic node recovery
Capacity Continuous provisioning and managed Karpenter autoscaling
Training Process-level recovery and managed tiered checkpointing
Inference Intelligent routing and tiered key-value (KV) caching
Storage & Registry Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon FSx for Lustre, and Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) to carry images, data, and checkpoints

This blog explores how this powerful native capability simplifies operations, enhances compliance tracking, and streamlines version management for enterprise-scale Kubernetes deployments.

🌐 The Multi-Cluster Management Challenge

Managing Kubernetes at scale has become increasingly complex for organizations running multiple clusters. As companies expand their containerized infrastructure footprint, they inevitably distribute clusters across different AWS regions and accounts for reasons including:

  • 🔄 Enhanced availability and failover capabilities
  • 🛡️ Business continuity requirements
  • 📍 Data sovereignty compliance

But this distributed approach creates a visibility nightmare. Without centralized monitoring, cluster administrators face several challenges:

  • 🔎 Limited cross-region and cross-account visibility
  • ⏱️ Time-consuming manual inventory tracking
  • 📝 Difficulty in assessing version compliance
  • 🧩 Fragmented operational planning

Many organizations have resorted to third-party solutions to address these issues, but these come with their own complications:

  • Complex identity and access management setup
  • Additional licensing costs
  • Ongoing maintenance overhead

🚀 Enter EKS Dashboard: Visibility Simplified

AWS has now addressed this pain point with the introduction of the Amazon EKS Dashboard—a native AWS Console capability that provides that long-desired “single pane of glass” for all your Kubernetes clusters.

The EKS Dashboard delivers comprehensive insights into three critical resource types:

  • 🔵 EKS clusters
  • 🟢 Managed node groups
